chunks: Types of PCBs, trade-offs and uses. The question: What are the different types of PCBs? What are their tradeoffs and applications?
A PCB (printed circuit board) is the flat board that holds electronic parts and links them with copper tracks.
Products need different things: cheap, small, bendable, or able to handle heat or radio signals.
Each type trades cost against density, performance or shape, so you pick the simplest one that does the job.
Think of buildings. A garden shed is cheap and fine for a few tools. An apartment tower packs many people onto a small plot, but costs far more.
A tent folds up and moves, but cannot carry much. The analogy breaks in one place: board features combine, so one board can be many-layered and bendable at once.
Cross-sections of six common types. Orange is copper, grey-green is dielectric or prepreg, purple is polyimide and the heavy grey base is aluminium.

Note the plated through-hole in the double-sided and multilayer boards, the tiny microvias and buried via in HDI, the thin bendable polyimide between rigid parts in rigid-flex, and the thin dielectric on a thick metal base in metal-core boards.
Layer count: how many copper layers the board has. More layers give more room for tracks and for solid power and ground sheets ("Choosing the PCB layer count").
FR-4: the standard fiberglass-and-epoxy board material, cheap and used for most boards ("What "FR4" means").
Flex board: a board built on thin bendable plastic (polyimide) instead of stiff fiberglass ("Flex PCBs: construction, trade-offs, uses"). HDI: high-density interconnect.
Tiny laser-drilled holes and fine tracks that pack parts closely. Metal-core board: copper over a very thin insulating layer on an aluminum base, which carries heat away well.
A TV remote has few parts and slow signals, so one copper layer is enough. That single-sided board is the cheapest type. A 3 watts LED is a different problem: heat.
Its heat must pass through the board's insulating layer to escape. Through 1.
6 mm of plain FR-4 under a 1 cm² pad, that layer alone would make the LED about 160 degrees Celsius hotter than the far side of the board.
A metal-core board's insulator is only 0. 1 mm thick and conducts heat better, so the rise is only about 1. 5 degrees Celsius.
Same job, different board, chosen by the requirement. That is the whole idea.
"By layer count: single-sided is cheapest for simple products, double-sided is the default, multilayer adds planes for signal integrity and density.
By rigidity: rigid, flex for bending, and rigid-flex combining both.
By material: FR-4 for most, PTFE or Rogers-type laminates for RF, ceramic for high temperature, metal-core with an aluminium base for LEDs and power.
And HDI with microvias for dense designs like phones. I'd choose the simplest type that meets density, thermal, RF and form-factor needs."
